module.title: Integration & Accumulation
module.destination: Build one-variable integration as signed accumulation from finite local contributions, Riemann-sum limits and FTC; derive structural substitution/integration-by-parts tools; audit proper/improper existence without M12+ machinery.
module.gate: S01 is the required pilot vertical slice. The full 20-session architecture is frozen only at the design level until this pilot passes Gates 4-8.
module.nextBoundary: M12 remains closed. Taylor/higher-order asymptotics are neither used nor authored.

owns: finite accumulation from local quantity times width (pilot scope only)
excludes: M12 Taylor polynomials/series, higher-order asymptotics and remainder theorems
optimization and a broad MVT applications unit
boundary.decisiveProhibition: Build M11 from M09 limits and M10 one-variable differential structure; never use M12+ machinery, measure theory, multivariable integration, numerical quadrature, L'Hopital, probability-density semantics or advanced integration tricks as a premise.

sessions.title: Finite accumulation is local quantity times width
sessions.focus: Construct a signed finite total from varying local rates/intensities before any integral notation exists.
sessions.purpose: Make accumulation a modelling operation rather than an antiderivative symbol: partitioned contribution = local quantity × interval width, then sum.
sessions.centralCapability: Construct and audit a finite signed accumulation sum with nonuniform widths, correct units and weighting.
sessions.principalObstacle: Learners often add or average sampled rates while ignoring unequal exposure widths, which produces dimensionally or numerically wrong totals.
requiredOwnership: Construct a finite signed accumulation as a sum of local quantity times interval width.
Track units from local quantity times width to the accumulated total.
Reject an unweighted sum or unweighted-rate average when interval widths are unequal.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite piecewise-constant one-variable accumulation only; no Riemann-limit or integral notation yet.
sessions.transferScope: Changed physical surface and representation requiring reconstruction of the same local-quantity × width architecture.
sessions.exitCondition: Solve both fixed tasks by constructing the weighted contributions, with no answer exposure; an unweighted solver must lose the relevant credit.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. A local rate or density tells you an amount per unit of input. A total over a finite piece must therefore combine two things: the local quantity and how much input-range that quantity acts over.
Define. For a finite list of pieces, write width_i for the size of piece i and q_i for its signed local quantity per input-unit. The contribution of that piece is q_i·width_i. The finite accumulated total is the sum of those contributions. If q_i is measured in units/hour and width_i in hours, their product is in units.
Connect. M10 interpreted a derivative as a local rate with output-units per input-unit. Here we do not yet take a continuum limit; we only ask how already-specified local rates contribute over finite pieces.
Explain. Unequal widths matter. Adding rates alone has the units of a rate, not a total. Taking an unweighted average of rates treats all pieces as equally wide even when they are not. Signs also matter: a negative local rate contributes negative change.
Worked example: an inventory changes at +8 units/hour for 0.5 h, -2 units/hour for 1.5 h, and +5 units/hour for 1 h. The contributions are +4 units, -3 units and +5 units, so the net change is +6 units. The widths total 3 h, and the width-weighted average rate is 6/3=2 units/hour. The ordinary average (8-2+5)/3=11/3 units/hour is a different quantity and does not reconstruct the net change.
Guided practice: a process adds material at 3 g/min for 2 min and then removes material at 1 g/min for 4 min. Write the two signed contributions before adding them. Check: +6 g and -4 g, giving +2 g net. Explain why the signs belong to the local rates while the interval widths stay positive.

sessions.title: Partitions, tags and mesh
sessions.focus: Formalize finite accumulation with partitions, tagged sample points, nonuniform widths and a refinement measure that cannot be fooled by interval count.
sessions.purpose: Give the learner precise finite-sum objects before any limiting definition.
sessions.centralCapability: Construct and audit a tagged finite sum on a nonuniform partition, including the mesh.
sessions.principalObstacle: The number of pieces can grow while one interval remains wide, so n→∞ alone does not describe genuine refinement for arbitrary partitions.
requiredOwnership: Construct a valid partition, subinterval widths and tags for a bounded interval.
Compute a tagged finite sum and its mesh on a nonuniform partition.
Explain why increasing the number of arbitrary subintervals does not by itself force refinement.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite tagged sums only; no definite-integral limit yet.
sessions.transferScope: Changed from sum computation to a pathological partition sequence where interval count grows but mesh does not shrink.
sessions.exitCondition: Main constructs the finite object correctly; Transfer rejects n→∞ as a sufficient refinement criterion.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. S01 used named pieces. To discuss every possible refinement later, we need a precise description of the pieces and sample locations.
Define. A partition of [a,b] is an ordered list P={x_0,...,x_n} with a=x_0<x_1<...<x_n=b. Subinterval i is [x_{i-1},x_i] and has positive width Δx_i=x_i-x_{i-1}. A tag t_i is any chosen point in that subinterval. The tagged finite sum is Σ_{i=1}^n f(t_i)Δx_i. The mesh ||P|| is max_i Δx_i, the width of the widest subinterval.
Connect. This is S01's local-quantity×width sum with the interval bookkeeping made explicit. Sigma notation compresses the sum; it does not change its meaning.
Explain. For arbitrary partitions, n is not a reliable measure of fineness. On [0,1], keep [0,1/2] intact and split only [1/2,1] into more and more pieces. The number of pieces grows without bound, but ||P|| remains 1/2.
Worked example: on [0,4], take P={0,1,2.5,4}; widths are 1,1.5,1.5, so ||P||=1.5. Choose tags 0.5,2,3.7 and suppose f at those tags is 2,-1,3. The tagged sum is 2(1)+(-1)(1.5)+3(1.5)=5.
Guided practice: for P={-2,-1,1,3} on [-2,3], list the widths before choosing any tags. Check: 1,2,2, hence ||P||=2. Explain why a tag for the middle subinterval must lie in [-1,1].

sessions.title: The definite integral is a common refinement limit
sessions.focus: Define the proper Riemann integral using arbitrarily fine tagged partitions and separate discovery of a candidate from proof of a common limit.
sessions.purpose: Turn S02 finite objects into the continuum accumulation object without relying on FTC.
sessions.centralCapability: State and use the tagged-partition definition of the definite integral.
sessions.principalObstacle: A learner may mistake convergence along one convenient regular grid for the stronger requirement that every sufficiently fine admissible tagged partition produces nearly the same total.
requiredOwnership: State the operational tagged-partition criterion for a proper Riemann integral.
Use that criterion to reconstruct a constant-function integral directly from sums.
Convert a uniform mesh-dependent error bound into an epsilon-delta integrability proof.
sessions.applicationScope: Bounded real functions on finite closed intervals; proper Riemann integral only.
sessions.transferScope: Changed from exact constant sums to a supplied all-partitions error certificate that must be converted into an epsilon argument.
sessions.exitCondition: The learner treats the integral as a common tagged-sum limit and can certify one from an explicit bound.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. A finite tagged sum depends on a partition and tags. A continuum total should not depend on which sufficiently fine partition happened to be chosen.
Define. For a bounded real function f on [a,b], say that f is Riemann integrable with integral I if for every ε>0 there is δ>0 such that every tagged partition with ||P||<δ satisfies |Σ f(t_i)Δx_i-I|<ε. We then write ∫_a^b f(x) dx=I. Here f is the integrand; x is a dummy variable of integration. The bounds a,b name the interval, not M09 limit values.
Connect. This is M09's accuracy-contract idea applied to the finite sums from S02. The mesh is the input control; the sum's distance from I is the output error.
Explain. One regular left-endpoint sequence can suggest I, but the definition asks for all sufficiently fine allowed tags/partitions. Discovery and proof are different jobs.
Worked example: if f(x)=2 on [-1,3], every tagged sum is Σ2Δx_i=2ΣΔx_i=2(4)=8, regardless of partition or tags. Therefore for any ε we may choose any δ>0: every sum equals 8 exactly, so ∫_{-1}^3 2 dx=8.
Guided practice: repeat the same argument for the constant function c on [a,b]. Check that ΣcΔx_i=c(b-a), because the subinterval widths telescope to b-a. Do not invoke an antiderivative.

sessions.title: Integrability diagnostics: point changes and tag dependence
sessions.focus: Use the definition to show why finite point changes can be harmless while persistent tag dependence can destroy Riemann integrability.
sessions.purpose: Break the false equivalence between 'discontinuous' and 'nonintegrable' and force partition-independent reasoning.
sessions.centralCapability: Diagnose elementary Riemann integrability or nonintegrability from uniform sum bounds and tag-choice counterexamples.
sessions.principalObstacle: Learners may treat continuity as necessary, or may accept one convergent sampling sequence despite other tags producing incompatible totals.
entryPrerequisites: continuous⇒Riemann-integrable theorem stated here as source-supported support
requiredOwnership: Show that finitely many bounded point-value changes can preserve a known Riemann integral by bounding their tagged-sum effect.
Refute Riemann integrability by constructing incompatible tagged sums on arbitrarily fine partitions.
Explain why discontinuity alone does not decide Riemann integrability.
sessions.applicationScope: Elementary bounded examples only; no general discontinuity-set criterion.
sessions.transferScope: Changed from finite exceptional points to a dense two-valued function with a supplied density fact.
sessions.exitCondition: The learner can produce both a discontinuous-but-integrable witness and a discontinuous-nonintegrable witness using the Riemann definition.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. OpenStax's standard sufficient theorem says every continuous real function on a closed interval is Riemann integrable. It is sufficient, not necessary, and M11 does not import its full compactness/uniform-continuity proof.
Define. A finite point change means two bounded functions differ only at finitely many input points. A tagged sum can notice such a point only through the one subinterval whose tag hits it.
Connect. If f and g differ only at one point c and |f(c)-g(c)|≤D, then on a partition of mesh m the exceptional point can be used as a tag in at most the two adjacent subintervals, so the tagged sums differ by at most 2Dm. All other tagged contributions match. As m→0 this discrepancy vanishes. Finitely many point changes give a finite sum of such bounds.
Explain. By contrast, if every subinterval permits two tag types that force different heights, arbitrarily fine partitions can still support incompatible sums. Then no common value can satisfy the S03 definition.
Worked example: let f(x)=2 on [-1,1] and let g equal 2 except g(0)=100. Any tagged sums differ only if the tag in the subinterval containing 0 is chosen as 0, and then the difference is at most 196||P||. Since f has integral 4, g also has integral 4.
Guided practice: if two bounded functions differ only at c with value gap at most 7, what mesh condition certainly makes their tagged sums differ by less than ε? Check: ||P||<ε/14. This controls sum discrepancy; it does not claim the functions are continuous.

sessions.title: Linearity, interval additivity and orientation
sessions.focus: Derive the basic algebra of the definite integral from finite-sum identities and M09 limit laws.
sessions.purpose: Make integral manipulation accountable to the Riemann structure before antiderivative shortcuts exist.
sessions.centralCapability: Use linearity, adjacent-interval additivity and interval orientation with signs intact.
sessions.principalObstacle: Learners often treat reversal as harmless, split intervals inconsistently, or apply algebra to integrals without knowing which identities are linear and which are not.
requiredOwnership: Use linearity of the definite integral for finite linear combinations.
Use additivity across adjacent intervals to reconstruct a total.
Apply the reversed-bound convention with the correct sign.
sessions.applicationScope: Proper Riemann integrals of already integrable functions on finite intervals.
sessions.transferScope: Changed to a contextual cumulative-flow ledger with no function formula, requiring structural composition and orientation.
outOfScope: nonlinear identities such as integral of a product
sessions.exitCondition: The learner combines and reverses known integrals without inventing nonlinear rules.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Once an integral exists, we need rules for combining accumulated quantities without rebuilding every tagged-sum limit from scratch.
Define. For integrable f and g and constants α,β on the same interval, linearity is ∫(αf+βg)=α∫f+β∫g. For a≤c≤b, adjacent-interval additivity is ∫_a^b f=∫_a^c f+∫_c^b f. We define ∫_a^a f=0 and ∫_b^a f=-∫_a^b f.
Connect. At the finite-sum level, Σ[αf(t_i)+βg(t_i)]Δx_i=αΣf(t_i)Δx_i+βΣg(t_i)Δx_i; M09 limit linearity carries this identity to the integral. Interval additivity comes from concatenating the pieces.
Explain. Reversing bounds changes orientation, so it changes the sign. Linearity does not create rules such as ∫fg=(∫f)(∫g); multiplication is not a linear operation.
Worked example: suppose ∫_0^2 f=4 and ∫_0^2 g=-1. Then ∫_0^2(3f-2g)=3(4)-2(-1)=14. Also, if ∫_0^1 f=1.5 and ∫_1^2 f=2.5, additivity recovers ∫_0^2 f=4 and reversal gives ∫_2^0 f=-4.
Guided practice: if ∫_1^3 q=-2 and ∫_3^5 q=7, first find ∫_1^5 q, then ∫_5^1 q. Check: 5 and -5. State which step uses additivity and which uses orientation.

sessions.title: Order, magnitude, cancellation and average value
sessions.focus: Use integral order structure to bound signed totals and separate net accumulation from total magnitude.
sessions.purpose: Prevent the area/magnitude intuition from erasing sign and give quantitative sanity checks before FTC evaluation.
sessions.centralCapability: Reason about bounds, absolute accumulation, cancellation and average value for proper integrals.
sessions.principalObstacle: A small signed integral can hide large positive and negative contributions, and absolute value cannot be moved through an integral as an equality.
requiredOwnership: Use pointwise bounds to bound a definite integral on a finite interval.
Distinguish signed accumulation ∫f from total magnitude ∫|f| and apply |∫f|≤∫|f|.
Compute the average value (1/(b-a))∫_a^b f for b>a.
sessions.applicationScope: Proper finite-interval integrals; average value is defined without invoking a mean-value existence theorem.
sessions.transferScope: Changed from explicit piecewise rates to abstract inequality certificates requiring order reasoning rather than direct accumulation arithmetic.
sessions.exitCondition: A wrong solver who equates signed and absolute accumulation or reverses comparison direction loses targeted credit.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Integral linearity tells us how totals combine; order tells us whether a proposed total is even plausible.
Define. If f(x)≤g(x) everywhere on [a,b] and both are integrable, then ∫f≤∫g. Hence m≤f≤M gives m(b-a)≤∫f≤M(b-a). For b>a, the average value is f_avg=(1/(b-a))∫_a^b f.
Connect. Because -|f|≤f≤|f|, integration preserves the inequalities: -∫|f|≤∫f≤∫|f|. Therefore |∫f|≤∫|f|. Equality is not automatic because positive and negative contributions can cancel in ∫f.
Explain. Signed accumulation answers net change. Integrating |f| answers accumulated magnitude in contexts where absolute rate has that meaning. Geometric area is therefore not the universal definition of an integral.
Worked example: a piecewise rate is +3 units/hour on [0,1] and -1 unit/hour on [1,4]. The signed total is 3(1)-1(3)=0 units, while the magnitude total is 3(1)+1(3)=6 units. The average signed rate over four hours is 0 units/hour.
Guided practice: if an integrable q satisfies 2≤q(x)≤5 on an interval of length 3, bound its integral before calculating anything else. Check: 6≤∫q≤15.

sessions.title: Accumulation functions are continuous before they are differentiable
sessions.focus: Turn one endpoint into a variable and use boundedness of a proper Riemann integrand to control changes in accumulated total.
sessions.purpose: Separate continuity of cumulative amount from the stronger FTC claim that its derivative equals the integrand.
sessions.centralCapability: Prove and use the continuity bound for A(x)=∫_a^x f when f is bounded/integrable.
sessions.principalObstacle: A jump in the local integrand can tempt the learner to predict a jump in the accumulated total, even though a point or short interval contributes vanishing total width.
entryPrerequisites: Riemann integrable functions are bounded on their finite domain
requiredOwnership: Derive a bound |A(y)-A(x)|≤M|y-x| from |f|≤M for an accumulation function.
Use the bound to prove continuity of an accumulation function without assuming f is continuous.
Distinguish continuity of accumulated total from differentiability at a jump of the integrand.
sessions.applicationScope: Proper accumulation functions of bounded Riemann-integrable real functions.
sessions.transferScope: Changed from an abstract bound to an explicit step-rate accumulation whose cumulative function stays continuous but has a corner.
sessions.exitCondition: The learner does not infer A'=f merely from continuity and can explain a continuous cumulative total across a bounded rate jump.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Define A(x)=∫_a^x f(t)dt. Before asking for A'(x), ask the weaker question: can A itself jump when x moves a tiny amount?
Define. A Riemann-integrable function on a finite closed interval is bounded, so choose M with |f(t)|≤M. For any x,y in the domain, interval additivity gives A(y)-A(x)=∫_x^y f(t)dt.
Connect. S06 gives |∫_x^y f|≤∫_x^y |f|≤M|y-x| (with orientation handled by absolute value). Thus |A(y)-A(x)|≤M|y-x|.
Explain. Given ε>0, taking |y-x|<ε/M (when M>0) makes |A(y)-A(x)|<ε. So A is continuous even if f itself has bounded jumps. This does not say A is differentiable at those jumps.
Worked example: let f(t)=1 for -1≤t<0 and f(t)=3 for 0≤t≤1, and A(x)=∫_{-1}^x f(t)dt. Then A(x)=x+1 for x≤0 and A(x)=1+3x for x≥0. Both formulas give A(0)=1, so A is continuous, but its left slope is 1 and right slope is 3.
Guided practice: if |q(t)|≤6 and Q(x)=∫_0^x q(t)dt, what bound controls |Q(2.01)-Q(2)|? Check: at most 6(0.01)=0.06. State what this proves about continuity, and what it does not prove about Q'(2).

sessions.title: FTC local recovery from a shrinking average
sessions.focus: Prove that the derivative of an accumulation function recovers the integrand at a point where the integrand is continuous.
sessions.purpose: Make the first FTC direction a theorem with a mechanism and hypotheses rather than symbolic cancellation.
sessions.centralCapability: Reconstruct the local-average proof that A'(c)=f(c) when f is integrable and continuous at c.
sessions.principalObstacle: The difference quotient is an average over a shrinking interval, not literally f(c); continuity is the step that turns nearby values into the point value.
requiredOwnership: Reconstruct the short-interval-average proof of A'(c)=f(c) under the stated continuity/integrability hypotheses.
Recover a local rate and its units from the derivative of a cumulative quantity.
Refuse FTC derivative recovery at a jump when the one-sided accumulated slopes disagree.
sessions.applicationScope: Proper Riemann-integrable f and points of continuity; interior-point proof, with one-sided endpoint variants only when explicitly stated.
sessions.transferScope: Changed to a cumulative dose model plus a jump-rate countercase requiring theorem-hypothesis auditing.
sessions.exitCondition: The learner can explain why the shrinking average tends to f(c) and can identify a discontinuity failure without declaring the accumulation undefined.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. S07 showed that A(x)=∫_a^x f is continuous. To get A'(c)=f(c), we need to understand its difference quotient.
Define. For h≠0 with c+h in the interval, [A(c+h)-A(c)]/h=(1/h)∫_c^{c+h} f(t)dt. This is the signed average value of f over the short interval from c to c+h.
Connect. Subtract f(c): [A(c+h)-A(c)]/h-f(c)=(1/h)∫_c^{c+h}[f(t)-f(c)]dt. If f is continuous at c, then for any ε>0 all sufficiently nearby t satisfy |f(t)-f(c)|<ε.
Explain. The integral bound gives the absolute difference between the short-interval average and f(c) at most ε, for positive or negative h. Therefore the difference quotient tends to f(c), so A'(c)=f(c). The Riemann integral must exist on the relevant intervals; continuity at c is the local hypothesis that drives derivative recovery.
Worked example: if f is continuous and f(2)=4, then for A(x)=∫_0^x f(t)dt the theorem gives A'(2)=4 without finding a formula for A. If f has a jump at c, S07 still gives a continuous accumulation, but the derivative can fail there.
Guided practice: suppose f is continuous at -1 with f(-1)=5 and B(x)=∫_3^x f(t)dt. What is B'(-1)? Check: 5. Explain why the fixed basepoint 3 disappears from the local difference quotient.

sessions.title: Moving endpoints without differentiating the integrand
sessions.focus: Compose FTC accumulation with M10's chain rule and interval orientation for variable upper/lower endpoints.
sessions.purpose: Extend the local recovery theorem to moving bounds while sharply separating it from parameter-dependent integrands.
sessions.centralCapability: Differentiate proper integrals with ordinary variable endpoints under explicit continuity/domain hypotheses.
sessions.principalObstacle: Leibniz-looking notation can tempt learners either to forget the endpoint chain factor or to differentiate the dummy-variable integrand with respect to x.
requiredOwnership: Differentiate a variable upper endpoint by composing an accumulation function with the endpoint map.
Differentiate an integral with two moving endpoints using orientation and two chain-rule contributions.
Distinguish moving-bound differentiation from differentiation under the integral sign.
sessions.applicationScope: Integrands independent of the outer variable; proper finite intervals; endpoint images remain in a region where the integrand is continuous.
sessions.transferScope: Changed from one composite upper endpoint to two independently moving endpoints and a dummy-variable misconception check.
sessions.exitCondition: Every endpoint contribution has the correct sign, evaluation point and chain factor; no derivative of the dummy integrand is invented.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. If A(y)=∫_a^y f(t)dt and f is continuous where needed, S08 gives A'(y)=f(y). Now let the endpoint itself depend on x.
Define. H(x)=∫_a^{g(x)}f(t)dt is A(g(x)), so M10's chain rule gives H'(x)=f(g(x))g'(x). For a lower endpoint, ∫_{g(x)}^a f=-A(g(x)), producing a minus sign.
Connect. Therefore J(x)=∫_{u(x)}^{v(x)}f(t)dt can be written A(v(x))-A(u(x)), so J'(x)=f(v(x))v'(x)-f(u(x))u'(x), provided the endpoint images stay where FTC applies.
Explain. The t in f(t) is a dummy integration variable. Nothing here differentiates an integrand that itself depends on x. That more general theorem is outside M11.
Worked example: H(x)=∫_1^{x²+1} cos t dt. Since cos is continuous, H'(x)=cos(x²+1)·2x. No antiderivative is required.
Guided practice: K(x)=∫_{x³}^2 e^t dt. Check K'(x)=-e^{x³}·3x². Identify the minus sign as lower-endpoint orientation, not as a derivative of e^t.

sessions.title: Antiderivative uniqueness needs an interval theorem
sessions.focus: Make the derivative-zero support theorem visible before using '+C' or FTC endpoint evaluation.
sessions.purpose: Establish only the MVT consequence needed to prove that antiderivatives of the same function differ by a constant on an interval.
sessions.centralCapability: Use the derivative-zero consequence of the Mean Value Theorem with its interval hypotheses to justify antiderivative uniqueness.
sessions.principalObstacle: The slogan 'same derivative means differ by C' feels algebraic, so the connected-interval and differentiability hypotheses are easily forgotten.
requiredOwnership: Use the Mean Value Theorem to prove that a function continuous on an interval and differentiable on its interior with zero derivative there is constant.
Use the derivative-zero result to justify that two antiderivatives of the same function differ by a constant on an interval.
Preserve the interval/domain hypothesis by diagnosing a disconnected-domain counterexample.
sessions.applicationScope: Real differentiable functions on intervals; the MVT appears only as a bounded support bridge.
sessions.transferScope: Changed from an interval theorem to a disconnected-domain counterexample where derivative zero holds componentwise but no single global constant exists.
sessions.exitCondition: The learner can justify +C on an interval and can state why the conclusion is componentwise on disconnected domains.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. To turn an antiderivative into a family F+C, we need a theorem: derivative zero on an interval forces no net change.
Define. For the interval theorem used here, H is continuous on an interval I and differentiable at every interior point of I. The Mean Value Theorem says: if u<v are points of I, then on [u,v] there is c∈(u,v) with H(v)-H(u)=H'(c)(v-u). An antiderivative F of f is understood on an interval where the needed continuity holds and F'=f on the interior.
Connect. The support chain is bounded: M10's derivative definition proves Fermat's interior-extremum lemma; M09's EVT plus Fermat gives Rolle's theorem; applying Rolle to H minus its secant line gives MVT. M11 will use only the next consequence.
Explain. If H is continuous on an interval and H'=0 at every interior point, take any u<v in it. MVT gives H(v)-H(u)=H'(c)(v-u)=0, so H(v)=H(u); H is constant. If F and G are continuous on the interval and F'=G'=f on its interior, then (F-G)'=0 there, hence F-G=C on that interval.
Worked example: F(x)=x²+3 and G(x)=x²-7 both differentiate to 2x on R. Their difference is 10, illustrating the theorem; the constant conclusion is not obtained by comparing one sample point alone but by the derivative-zero argument on the interval.
Guided practice: suppose U' and V' both equal q on an interval I and U(2)-V(2)=5. What is U(x)-V(x) for every x∈I? Check: 5, because the difference has derivative zero.

sessions.title: FTC endpoint evaluation and net change
sessions.focus: Use the accumulation derivative plus antiderivative uniqueness to derive endpoint evaluation, then interpret it as net change.
sessions.purpose: Close the two-way bridge between local derivative information and proper accumulated totals without redefining the integral as an antiderivative.
sessions.centralCapability: Reconstruct and apply the endpoint-evaluation form of FTC under explicit continuity hypotheses.
sessions.principalObstacle: Endpoint brackets are often memorized as the definition of integration, obscuring both the prior Riemann definition and why additive constants cancel.
requiredOwnership: Reconstruct FTC endpoint evaluation from the accumulation function and antiderivative uniqueness.
Evaluate a proper definite integral with a verified antiderivative without adding an arbitrary constant to the final number.
Use the integral of a rate as net change between endpoint states.
sessions.applicationScope: Continuous integrands on finite closed intervals and verified antiderivatives.
sessions.transferScope: Changed from theorem reconstruction/exact integral to a signed state-change model with an initial condition.
sessions.exitCondition: The learner can say why F(b)-F(a) is legal and can move between rate and state change.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. S03 defined the integral from sums. S08 showed that an accumulation A(x)=∫_a^x f has derivative f when f is continuous. S10 now lets us compare A with any other antiderivative.
Define. If f is continuous on [a,b] and F'=f there, define A(x)=∫_a^x f(t)dt. S08 gives A'=f on the interior. Hence (F-A)'=0, so S10 makes F-A constant on the interval.
Connect. At x=a, A(a)=0, so F(x)-A(x)=F(a). Therefore A(b)=F(b)-F(a), i.e. ∫_a^b f(x)dx=F(b)-F(a). This is a theorem built on the Riemann integral, not its definition.
Explain. Replacing F by F+C changes both endpoint values by C, which cancels. Thus +C belongs to the antiderivative family, not to the numerical definite integral.
Worked example: for f(x)=2x on [1,3], F(x)=x² is an antiderivative, so ∫_1^3 2x dx=9-1=8. A differentiation check verifies F'=2x.
Guided practice: evaluate ∫_0^2 3x² dx using F=x³. Check: 8. Then explain why (x³+17)|_0^2 gives the same result.

sessions.title: A small antiderivative repertoire, verified by differentiation
sessions.focus: Reverse only derivative facts already available from M10, preserving constants and original domains.
sessions.purpose: Create enough exact evaluation fluency for later M11 transformations/improper limits without turning the module into an integration-trick catalogue.
sessions.centralCapability: Assemble and verify elementary antiderivatives from established derivative pairs with domain conditions visible.
sessions.principalObstacle: Formula-table memory encourages wrong signs, missing logarithmic domains and antiderivatives that cross points where the integrand is undefined.
requiredOwnership: Construct an elementary antiderivative on a stated interval from the established repertoire.
Verify a proposed antiderivative by differentiating it back to the integrand.
Preserve interval/domain restrictions, especially for 1/x and negative powers.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite linear combinations of powers already justified from M10, e^x/b^x, sin/cos and 1/x on legal intervals.
sessions.transferScope: Changed to a negative-power/base-exponential combination on a negative interval, forcing domain preservation and derivative verification.
sessions.exitCondition: The learner verifies rather than merely recognizes formulas and never bridges across an excluded point with one antiderivative interval.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. FTC makes antiderivatives computationally useful, but M11 needs only a small repertoire that can be checked from M10.
Define. An indefinite-integral expression ∫f(x)dx=F(x)+C abbreviates the antiderivative family on a stated interval; it is not a definite integral. Constants combine by linearity.
Connect. Reverse verified M10 derivatives: d(x^{n+1}/(n+1))/dx=x^n for integer n≠-1 on its legal domain; d(e^x)/dx=e^x; d(b^x/ln b)/dx=b^x for b>0,b≠1; d(sin x)/dx=cos x; d(-cos x)/dx=sin x. Since d(ln x)/dx=1/x for x>0 and d(ln(-x))/dx=1/x for x<0, an intervalwise shorthand is ln|x|+C for 1/x on intervals not crossing 0.
Explain. The safest check is differentiation. A formula that differentiates correctly where the original integrand is undefined still cannot create a legal antiderivative across the excluded point.
Worked example: on x>0, an antiderivative of 2x+3e^x-4/x is x²+3e^x-4ln x+C. Differentiation returns 2x+3e^x-4/x.
Guided practice: verify that -3cos x+2sin x differentiates to 3sin x+2cos x. Then state that adding any constant changes no derivative.

sessions.title: Substitution is the chain rule run backward
sessions.focus: Derive the one-variable substitution pattern from a verified composition derivative rather than from symbolic du cancellation.
sessions.purpose: Make the transformation structurally accountable before definite bounds are introduced.
sessions.centralCapability: Recognize and execute reverse-chain antiderivatives, including the derivative scale factor, and verify the result.
sessions.principalObstacle: A learner may replace an inner expression by u while forgetting that the differential scale must also match the inner derivative.
requiredOwnership: Recognize a reverse-chain integrand f(g(x))g'(x) and choose the inner transformation.
Carry the derivative scale factor correctly through an indefinite substitution.
Verify a substitution result by differentiating it in the original variable.
sessions.applicationScope: One-variable proper/indefinite transformations whose needed outer antiderivative is in the established repertoire.
sessions.transferScope: Changed to an error-diagnosis task where a missing scale factor produces a plausible but wrong antiderivative.
sessions.exitCondition: A learner cannot earn substitution ownership merely by naming u; the scale factor and backward derivative check must be correct.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. M10 says d/dx F(g(x))=F'(g(x))g'(x). Integration can reverse exactly that structure.
Define. If F'=f, then F(g(x)) is an antiderivative of f(g(x))g'(x). Writing u=g(x) and du=g'(x)dx abbreviates this chain-rule relationship; du is not a freely cancellable symbol.
Connect. The job is to identify the inner expression g(x), locate its derivative factor, and account for any constant mismatch before using the outer antiderivative.
Explain. If the integrand contains only half of g'(x), the answer needs the corresponding half factor. After substitution, differentiate the proposed result back in x; this catches missing scales.
Worked example: ∫2x(x²+1)^3 dx. Let u=x²+1, du=2x dx. Then ∫u³du=u⁴/4+C=(x²+1)^4/4+C. Differentiation returns 2x(x²+1)^3.
Guided practice: for ∫3x² e^{x³}dx, choose u=x³. Check that du=3x²dx and the antiderivative is e^{x³}+C.

sessions.title: Definite substitution transforms bounds and orientation
sessions.focus: Apply substitution directly to definite integrals with transformed endpoint values, sign/orientation and domain hypotheses intact.
sessions.purpose: Prevent mixed-variable bounds and sign errors while clarifying that this one-dimensional chain-rule identity does not require an inverse-Jacobian story.
sessions.centralCapability: Execute and audit definite one-variable substitution with transformed bounds.
sessions.principalObstacle: Learners often change the integrand to u but retain x-bounds, or reorder transformed bounds without changing sign.
requiredOwnership: Transform definite-integration bounds consistently under u=g(x).
Preserve orientation when the transformed endpoint order reverses.
Check the continuity/domain conditions needed by the transformed integrand.
sessions.applicationScope: One-variable proper substitutions justified by chain rule/FTC.
sessions.transferScope: Changed to a decreasing transformation whose new bounds reverse, with an explicit wrong-sign diagnosis.
sessions.exitCondition: No solution mixes u-integrands with x-bounds or silently flips reversed transformed limits.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. For definite integrals, substitution changes not only the expression but also the endpoint values.
Define. If u=g(x), then x=a maps to u=g(a) and x=b maps to u=g(b). Under the established chain/FTC hypotheses, ∫_a^b f(g(x))g'(x)dx=∫_{g(a)}^{g(b)}f(u)du.
Connect. The formula follows by taking an antiderivative F of f: both sides equal F(g(b))-F(g(a)). In this form no global inverse of g is needed. Domain and continuity of the actual expressions still matter.
Explain. If g(b)<g(a), the u-bounds are reversed and the integral can be negative. You may reorder them only by introducing a minus sign. Never keep x-bounds after changing the integration variable to u.
Worked example: ∫_0^1 2x e^{x²}dx. With u=x², the bounds 0→1 stay 0→1, giving ∫_0^1 e^u du=e-1.
Guided practice: ∫_0^1 -2x(3-x²)dx. Let u=3-x², so bounds 3→2. Check: ∫_3^2 u du=(4-9)/2=-5/2, matching the negative integrand.

sessions.title: Integration by parts is the product rule accumulated
sessions.focus: Derive integration by parts from M10's product rule and FTC, then preserve definite boundary terms.
sessions.purpose: Teach reverse-product structure rather than a mnemonic formula detached from its origin.
sessions.centralCapability: Reconstruct and apply integration by parts with a productive factor split and correct boundary terms.
sessions.principalObstacle: Learners may multiply antiderivatives, drop boundary terms, or choose a split whose 'v' is not available.
requiredOwnership: Reconstruct the integration-by-parts identity from the product rule and FTC.
Choose a workable differentiated/integrated factor split within the available antiderivative repertoire.
Carry definite boundary terms with correct signs.
sessions.applicationScope: One-variable proper integrals with verified factor derivatives/antiderivatives.
sessions.transferScope: Changed to auditing a completed definite calculation that drops or mis-signs the boundary/product contribution.
sessions.exitCondition: The learner can derive the identity and a wrong product/boundary solver loses targeted credit.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. There is no rule ∫uv=(∫u)(∫v). The useful product structure comes from accumulating the derivative product rule.
Define. M10 gives (uv)'=u'v+uv'. Integrate and use FTC: ∫u v' dx=uv-∫u'v dx. With du=u'dx and dv=v'dx, this is written ∫u dv=uv-∫v du. On [a,b], ∫_a^b u v' dx=[uv]_a^b-∫_a^b u'v dx.
Connect. Choose the factor to differentiate so it becomes simpler, and choose dv only when its antiderivative v is actually available. The identity trades one integral for another; it does not guarantee improvement.
Explain. In a definite integral, [uv]_a^b is part of the theorem. Dropping it changes the quantity.
Worked example: ∫_0^1 x e^x dx=[xe^x]_0^1-∫_0^1 e^x dx=e-(e-1)=1.
Guided practice: for ∫x cos x dx, take u=x and dv=cos x dx. Check: x sin x+cos x+C. Differentiate it to verify.

sessions.title: Method forensics: transform only when structure matches
sessions.focus: Choose among direct FTC, substitution, integration by parts or no current elementary exact method, and verify the choice.
sessions.purpose: Prevent the technique catalogue from becoming a guessing game and teach that legal transformations must actually simplify the task.
sessions.centralCapability: Diagnose integral structure and choose a justified method from the M11 toolkit without inventing unsupported machinery.
sessions.principalObstacle: Mnemonic-driven learners may force substitution or parts onto every integral and confuse 'a technique exists' with 'this technique improves the problem.'
requiredOwnership: Choose direct evaluation, substitution or integration by parts from the integrand's derivative structure.
Recognize when none of the current exact elementary tools has been justified instead of fabricating an antiderivative.
Verify a selected antiderivative by differentiating it back to the integrand.
sessions.applicationScope: Only the established M11 repertoire; no claim that an integral has no antiderivative in any broader mathematical sense.
sessions.transferScope: Changed to auditing a proposed method whose required intermediate antiderivative is unavailable and a second method that reduces the structure immediately.
sessions.exitCondition: The learner can say 'not with the current exact toolkit' precisely and can defend method choice structurally.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Substitution and parts are identities, not rituals. Ask what derivative structure is present and whether the transformation makes the remaining integral simpler.
Define. Direct: the integrand is already in S12's derivative-pair repertoire. Substitution: an inner expression and its derivative scale are present. Parts: a product can trade a derivative from one factor to another and v is available. None-current: no taught exact route is justified.
Connect. Verification is part of selection: differentiate an indefinite result, or check sign/bounds for a definite one.
Explain. 'None-current' does not mean the definite integral does not exist. It means M11 has not established an elementary exact antiderivative/technique for it. Numerical quadrature and special functions are outside this module.
Worked example: ∫2x cos(x²)dx suggests substitution; ∫x e^x dx suggests parts; ∫(3x²-4)dx is direct; ∫e^{x²}dx has no exact method in the current repertoire.
Guided practice: classify ∫x/(x²+5)dx (substitution), ∫x sin x dx (parts), and ∫e^{-x²}dx (none-current exact toolkit). Do not approximate the last one.

sessions.title: Infinite intervals are limits, not endpoints
sessions.focus: Define infinite-bound improper integrals through finite truncations and derive the p-tail threshold without L'Hôpital or M12 asymptotics.
sessions.purpose: Make existence the first question whenever an integral has an infinite interval.
sessions.centralCapability: Rewrite and decide representative infinite-tail improper integrals using M09 limits and FTC.
sessions.principalObstacle: Endpoint notation can tempt learners to substitute ∞ into an antiderivative as if infinity were a real number, hiding the convergence claim.
requiredOwnership: Rewrite an infinite-upper-bound integral as a limit of proper finite-bound integrals before evaluating it.
Derive the threshold ∫_1^∞ x^{-p}dx converges exactly when p>1.
Distinguish convergence to a finite value from divergence and reject literal substitution of infinity.
sessions.applicationScope: One-sided infinite intervals with positive power-law tails and elementary transforms.
sessions.transferScope: Changed from abstract p-tail proof to a shifted long-tail weight whose total must be judged by substitution to the p-tail form.
sessions.exitCondition: The learner explicitly writes the truncation limit and handles p=1 separately.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. The symbol ∞ is not a real endpoint. An expression ∫_a^∞ f asks whether a sequence/limit of finite accumulated totals settles to a finite value.
Define. ∫_a^∞ f(x)dx means lim_{T→∞}∫_a^T f(x)dx, provided that finite limit exists. If it does not, the improper integral diverges.
Connect. For x>0 and real α, M10's logarithm/exponential structure gives x^α=e^{αln x}, so d(x^α)/dx=αx^{α-1}. Thus for p≠1 an antiderivative of x^{-p} is x^{1-p}/(1-p); for p=1 it is ln x.
Explain. On [1,T], p≠1 gives (T^{1-p}-1)/(1-p). If p>1, 1-p<0 and T^{1-p}→0, giving 1/(p-1). If p<1, the positive total grows without bound. At p=1, ln T→∞. Therefore the p-tail converges exactly for p>1.
Worked example: ∫_1^∞ x^{-2}dx=lim_{T→∞}[-1/x]_1^T=1. The statement is a limit result; '-1/∞=0' is shorthand at best, not the definition.
Guided practice: write ∫_3^∞ x^{-3}dx as a T-limit and evaluate it. Check: [-1/(2x²)]_3^T→1/18.

sessions.title: Singular endpoints and interior breaks require separate limits
sessions.focus: Define finite-interval improper integrals at unbounded singularities and derive the near-zero p threshold.
sessions.purpose: Prevent a zero-width-point intuition or endpoint-bracket calculation from hiding divergent singular behavior.
sessions.centralCapability: Identify every singular endpoint, split interior singularities and decide representative one-sided convergence.
sessions.principalObstacle: A learner may treat an unbounded point like a harmless finite point change, or evaluate an antiderivative straight across a point where the integrand is undefined.
requiredOwnership: Rewrite an endpoint-singular integral as a one-sided limit and derive ∫_0^1 x^{-p}dx converges exactly when p<1.
Split an interior singularity into two one-sided improper integrals and require both to converge.
Reject direct endpoint evaluation across an undefined singular point.
sessions.applicationScope: Positive power singularities and elementary interior singularities.
sessions.transferScope: Changed from endpoint p-threshold to a rational integrand with an interior pole and a tempting finite endpoint-bracket answer.
outOfScope: Cauchy principal value as a developed theory
sessions.exitCondition: The learner lists every problematic side before doing algebra and never lets cancellation across a singularity certify ordinary convergence.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. A single point has zero width only when the integrand stays bounded. An unbounded singularity can make nearby accumulated mass arbitrarily large.
Define. If f is proper on (0,b], define ∫_0^b f=lim_{ε→0+}∫_ε^b f when that finite limit exists. If f has an interior singularity c, define ∫_a^b f as ∫_a^c f+∫_c^b f only when both one-sided improper integrals converge separately.
Connect. For x^{-p} on (0,1], p≠1 gives ∫_ε^1x^{-p}dx=(1-ε^{1-p})/(1-p). If p<1, ε^{1-p}→0 and the integral is 1/(1-p). If p>1 it diverges to +∞; p=1 gives -ln ε→∞.
Explain. Thus the near-zero threshold is p<1, the opposite inequality from the tail threshold. Directly plugging a singular endpoint into an antiderivative is not legal.
Worked example: ∫_0^1 x^{-1/2}dx=lim_{ε→0+}[2sqrt(x)]_ε^1=2. But ∫_0^1 dx/x diverges because -ln ε→∞.
Guided practice: for ∫_{-1}^1 1/sqrt(|x|) dx, identify two one-sided integrals at 0. Each converges to 2, so the total is 4; the split is part of the definition.

sessions.title: Comparison and cancellation forensics
sessions.focus: Use nonnegative comparison to decide convergence when exact evaluation is unnecessary, and reject symmetric cancellation as ordinary two-sided improper convergence.
sessions.purpose: Make existence proofs robust when antiderivatives are inconvenient and close the main improper-integral escape route.
sessions.centralCapability: Apply comparison in the correct direction and audit two-sided improper convergence separately from symmetric truncation.
sessions.principalObstacle: Learners reverse comparison implications or mistake cancellation of divergent left/right pieces for a convergent ordinary improper integral.
requiredOwnership: Use the nonnegative improper comparison theorem in the correct convergence/divergence direction.
Require both one-sided tails to converge for an ordinary integral over (-∞,∞).
Distinguish a symmetric cancellation limit from ordinary improper convergence.
sessions.applicationScope: Nonnegative comparison on tails and an elementary signed two-sided counterexample.
sessions.transferScope: Changed from nonnegative comparison tasks to an odd signed integrand whose symmetric truncations cancel while both one-sided integrals diverge.
outOfScope: principal-value theory beyond naming the distinction
sessions.exitCondition: A wrong comparison direction or symmetric-zero solver loses direct evidence.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Exact antiderivatives are not always needed: inequalities can transfer convergence information, but only in safe directions.
Define. For x≥a, if 0≤f(x)≤g(x) and ∫_a^∞g converges, then ∫_a^∞f converges. If ∫_a^∞f diverges to +∞, then the larger nonnegative g also diverges.
Connect. For each finite T, order gives 0≤F(T)=∫_a^T f≤G(T)=∫_a^T g. If G(T) is bounded above and F(T) is nondecreasing, M09's monotone-bounded convergence gives a finite limit. The divergence direction follows from G(T)≥F(T).
Explain. For ∫_{-∞}^{∞}f, choose any finite split point c and require both ∫_{-∞}^c f and ∫_c^∞ f to converge finitely. A symmetric limit lim_{R→∞}∫_{-R}^R f may exist by cancellation even when those one-sided requirements fail; that is not ordinary improper convergence.
Worked example: for x≥1, 0≤1/(x²+1)≤1/x², and the p=2 tail converges, so ∫_1^∞1/(x²+1)dx converges without needing its exact value.
Guided practice: for x≥1, sqrt(x²+1)≤sqrt(2)x, so 1/sqrt(x²+1)≥1/(sqrt(2)x). Since the harmonic tail diverges, the larger integrand's tail diverges too.

sessions.title: Synthesis: from local quantity to justified accumulated total
sessions.focus: Choose and connect the full M11 machinery: finite local contributions, proper integration, FTC recovery, structural transformation and improper-existence auditing.
sessions.purpose: Make the learner organize M11 as one accumulation system rather than a list of integral formulas.
sessions.centralCapability: Build, evaluate and audit one-variable accumulated quantities while distinguishing local rate, finite total and existence claims.
sessions.principalObstacle: A learner may know every individual formula yet still conflate local rate with total change, choose a technique without structural justification, or normalize an improper total before proving it is finite.
requiredOwnership: Connect a tagged local-quantity×width sum to the continuum accumulated total and preserve units.
Choose and justify a legal exact method for a proper accumulated total, then connect the result back to the state variable.
Use FTC locally with its continuity hypothesis while distinguishing local rate from interval net change.
Audit an infinite-domain accumulated total for existence before solving for its scale parameter.
sessions.applicationScope: One-variable proper and elementary improper accumulation using only the established M11 toolkit.
sessions.transferScope: Changed from a finite-time signed-rate state model to a scaled infinite-domain weight whose finite total exists only on a parameter region.
sessions.exitCondition: The learner selects the needed layer—finite sum, proper integral, FTC or improper existence—before calculation and states the relevant hypotheses.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. M11 began with local quantity×width and ends by asking which mathematical layer a total actually needs: a finite sum, a proper continuum limit, an FTC local-recovery claim, a structural transformation or an improper-existence audit.
Define. A local rate has output-units per input-unit. A finite contribution has output-units after multiplication by width. A proper definite integral is the partition-independent continuum total on a finite interval. An improper integral is an additional limit claim and must exist before it can be used as a finite total.
Connect. FTC links local and cumulative descriptions in both directions under its hypotheses: an accumulation derivative recovers a continuous integrand locally, while a verified antiderivative evaluates a proper accumulated total globally. Substitution and integration by parts are derived transformations, not definitions of integration.
Explain. Method choice follows structure. Reverse chain suggests substitution; reverse product suggests parts; direct derivative pairs need neither. Infinite or singular domains first require an existence limit. A local derivative value and an interval integral usually have different units and answer different questions.
Worked example: let A(x)=5+∫_0^x 3t² dt for 0≤x≤2. A finite tagged sum Σ3t_i²Δt approximates accumulated change in the units of A. FTC evaluation gives A(2)=5+[t³]_0^2=13. Local recovery gives A'(2)=12 in A-units per input-unit. The numbers 8 and 12 are not competing answers: one is interval net change, the other a local rate.
Guided practice: before evaluating ∫_0^∞ C(1+x)^(-2)dx, state the improper-limit question. Check: the shifted p=2 tail has finite base total 1, so a required finite total K would use C=K. This is plain accumulation arithmetic; no probability interpretation is being introduced.

T22V3::ARC510::S01-M@1.prompt: A battery system is observed over three consecutive intervals. Its signed net charging rate is +12 W for 0.25 h, -4 W for 0.75 h, and +6 W for 0.50 h. Construct the finite accumulation sum for the net energy change, compute that change, and state its units. Then explain why simply averaging the three rate values and multiplying by the total elapsed time is not a valid calculation for these unequal interval widths.

T22V3::ARC510::S01-T@1.prompt: A cable has three sections of lengths 0.8 m, 0.3 m, and 1.1 m. A piecewise-constant linear mass density model assigns 2 kg/m, 5 kg/m, and 1 kg/m to those sections respectively. Build the finite sum that represents the cable's modeled mass and compute it. A report instead adds 2+5+1 and calls the result '8 kg'; identify both the structural error and the unit error.

T22V3::ARC510::S02-M@1.prompt: On [1,6], let P={1,2,4.5,6}. Use tags t_1=1.4, t_2=3, t_3=5.2, and suppose f(t_1)=4, f(t_2)=-2, f(t_3)=1. List the three subinterval widths, verify that each tag is legal, compute Σ f(t_i)Δx_i, and state ||P||.

T22V3::ARC510::S02-T@1.prompt: For each n≥1, partition [0,1] by keeping [0,1/3] as one subinterval and dividing [1/3,1] into n equal subintervals. The number of subintervals tends to infinity. Determine the mesh ||P_n|| and explain why this sequence does not make the whole interval arbitrarily fine. State what refinement condition would repair the problem.

T22V3::ARC510::S03-M@1.prompt: Using the tagged-partition definition rather than FTC or an antiderivative, prove that the constant function f(x)=-3 on [2,5] has definite integral -9. Your argument must apply to every tagged partition, not only equal-width partitions.

T22V3::ARC510::S03-T@1.prompt: Suppose a bounded function g on [0,2] has the following proved property: for every tagged partition P, |S(g;P,t)-7|≤5||P||. Use only this certificate and the Riemann-integral definition to prove ∫_0^2 g(x)dx=7. Give an explicit δ in terms of ε.

T22V3::ARC510::S04-M@1.prompt: Define g on [0,3] by g(x)=5 for x≠1 and g(1)=-20. Using tagged sums and a mesh bound, prove that g is Riemann integrable and find its integral. Then state whether this example is continuous everywhere.

T22V3::ARC510::S04-T@1.prompt: On [0,1], define h(x)=1 when x is rational and h(x)=0 when x is irrational. You may use the supplied fact that every nonempty interval contains both rational and irrational numbers. For an arbitrary partition, construct two legal tag choices whose Riemann sums disagree by 1, and use them to show h is not Riemann integrable. Finally, explain what the Main/Transfer pair shows about the claim 'every discontinuous function is nonintegrable.'

T22V3::ARC510::S05-M@1.prompt: Suppose f and g are integrable and you are given ∫_1^4 f(x)dx=5, ∫_4^7 f(x)dx=-2, and ∫_1^7 g(x)dx=3. Compute (i) ∫_1^7 f, (ii) ∫_7^1 f, and (iii) ∫_1^7 [2f(x)-3g(x)]dx. Name the structural law used at each step.

T22V3::ARC510::S05-T@1.prompt: A signed flow model has accumulated +6 L from hour 0 to hour 2 and -4 L from hour 2 to hour 5 for component A. Component B accumulates +3 L from hour 0 to hour 5. Without inventing pointwise rate formulas, determine (i) A's accumulation from 0 to 5, (ii) A's accumulation from 5 back to 0 under the oriented convention, and (iii) the 0-to-5 accumulation of the combined rate 2A-B.

T22V3::ARC510::S06-M@1.prompt: A signed velocity model is v(t)=4 km/h on 0≤t≤1.5 and v(t)=-2 km/h on 1.5<t≤3.5. Compute (i) ∫_0^3.5 v(t)dt, (ii) ∫_0^3.5 |v(t)|dt, and (iii) the average value of v over [0,3.5]. Explain in one sentence why the first two totals differ.

T22V3::ARC510::S06-T@1.prompt: Let q be integrable on [2,6] and suppose -1≤q(x)≤3 for every x. Also suppose ∫_2^6 |q(x)|dx=5. Give the sharp bounds that follow immediately for ∫_2^6 q(x)dx from (a) the pointwise bounds and (b) the absolute-value inequality. Combine the information to state the tightest interval you can certify for the signed integral.

T22V3::ARC510::S07-M@1.prompt: Let g be Riemann integrable on [0,5] with |g(t)|≤7, and define G(x)=∫_2^x g(t)dt. Prove that |G(y)-G(x)|≤7|y-x| for all x,y∈[0,5], and use the bound to prove G is continuous. Do not assume g itself is continuous.

T22V3::ARC510::S07-T@1.prompt: A signed rate is h(t)=2 for 0≤t<1 and h(t)=-1 for 1≤t≤3. Define H(x)=∫_0^x h(t)dt. Find H(x) on 0≤x≤1 and on 1≤x≤3. Is H continuous at x=1? Is H differentiable there? Justify the differentiability answer from one-sided slopes rather than from a cancellation slogan.

T22V3::ARC510::S08-M@1.prompt: Let f be Riemann integrable on [-1,4], continuous at c=2, and satisfy f(2)=-3. Define A(x)=∫_{-1}^x f(t)dt. Reconstruct the local proof that A'(2)=-3: write the difference quotient as a short-interval average and use continuity at 2 to control its error.

T22V3::ARC510::S08-T@1.prompt: A cumulative dose is C(t)=∫_0^t r(s)ds, where r is measured in mg/min. First suppose r is continuous at t=5 and r(5)=2.4 mg/min. Find C'(5) and its units. Now instead suppose r is bounded and integrable but has left-hand values tending to 2 mg/min and right-hand values tending to 4 mg/min at t=5. State what remains true about C at t=5 and whether C'(5) exists, with a reason.

T22V3::ARC510::S09-M@1.prompt: Define F(x)=∫_0^{3x-1} e^{t²}dt. Without trying to find an elementary antiderivative of e^{t²}, find F'(x) and evaluate F'(1). State the continuity/domain fact that makes the endpoint rule legal.

T22V3::ARC510::S09-T@1.prompt: Let J(x)=∫_{x²}^{2x+1} ln(1+t²)dt. Find J'(x), keeping the upper- and lower-endpoint contributions separate. Then explain why differentiating ln(1+t²) with respect to x is not part of this calculation.

T22V3::ARC510::S10-M@1.prompt: Let I be an interval. Let F and G be continuous on I and differentiable at every interior point of I, with F'(x)=G'(x) at every interior point. Using the Mean Value Theorem as stated in the lesson, prove that F-G is constant on I. Then explain how this proves that two antiderivatives of one function on an interval differ by an additive constant.

T22V3::ARC510::S10-T@1.prompt: Define H on D=(-∞,0)∪(0,∞) by H(x)=0 for x<0 and H(x)=1 for x>0. Show that H'(x)=0 at every point of D, yet H is not one constant on all of D. Identify exactly which hypothesis from the S10 derivative-zero theorem fails, and state the correct componentwise conclusion.

T22V3::ARC510::S11-M@1.prompt: Assume f is continuous on [a,b]. Let F be continuous on [a,b] with F'(x)=f(x) for a<x<b, and define A(x)=∫_a^x f(t)dt. Using S08 and S10, reconstruct why ∫_a^b f(x)dx=F(b)-F(a). Then apply the theorem to evaluate ∫_{-1}^{2}(4x³-2x)dx with a verified antiderivative.

T22V3::ARC510::S11-T@1.prompt: A storage level Q(t) has rate Q'(t)=4t-10 liters/hour for 0≤t≤3, and Q(0)=50 liters. Use net-change integration to find Q(3). Also state why adding the positive and negative rate portions separately would give the same net result if done correctly.

T22V3::ARC510::S12-M@1.prompt: On the interval x>0, find an antiderivative family for f(x)=3x²-4e^x+2cos x+5/x. Differentiate your result to verify it, and state why the interval condition matters for the logarithmic term.

T22V3::ARC510::S12-T@1.prompt: On the interval x<0, find and verify an antiderivative of q(x)=2/x³+3·2^x. State why your formula is an intervalwise antiderivative on x<0 rather than evidence of one antiderivative defined across x=0.
